candidates.title: A $20 Paper Calendar Holds Three Months Without a Separate Stand
candidates.full_text:
TriAngular makes a calendar out of a narrow paper triangle, which sounds like a stationery trick until you consider the desk it’s meant to occupy. Between a laptop, a notebook, and whatever charging cable has claimed permanent residency, another stand feels like a commitment. A calendar that supports itself and keeps nearby months accessible makes a reasonable case for that remaining patch of space.

From stationery brand Replug, the TriAngular Calendar 2027 is listed at $20. Three months wrap around three faces, so checking another month means rotating the calendar. That addresses a second, smaller frustration: reaching for a phone just to find out which weekday a date falls on. You don’t see every face simultaneously, but neighboring months remain a turn away.

The construction is my favorite detail. The paper forms the triangular structure, held together with a clip that’s also made of paper. There’s no separate base to disguise or decorative frame to justify. Folding gives the printed sheet its support. I appreciate a design where the interesting shape earns its place through a practical job, especially when that job is as unglamorous as standing upright.

At 2.4 inches wide, 4.9 inches tall, and 2.1 inches deep, it’s small enough to consider for a desk where space is already negotiated inch by inch. The upright proportions are sensible: the information rises above the surface rather than spreading across it. I’d rather give a date reference a narrow vertical presence than sacrifice a broad rectangle of working space.

The silver material is specialty paper, rather than a metal casing. Replug says the calendar is hand-silkscreened, with sheets individually dried and white ink applied twice on silver paper. Made in Japan, it brings a little printmaking craft to an everyday object. That attention seems appropriate for something whose appearance depends so heavily on numerals and their background. There’s very little else for the printing to hide behind.

Compared with Google Calendar, which supports shared schedules, dated tasks, and events pulled from Gmail, TriAngular has a much narrower role. Google’s product makes sense for coordinating appointments and keeping other people informed. The paper triangle is for checking dates while you’re already doing something else. I wouldn’t abandon a digital calendar for it, but I can see the appeal of letting a separate object handle that quick reference.

Each month has perforations so it can be removed once it’s passed. January and February 2028 are included, keeping the calendar useful for looking ahead at the end of 2027. The tear-away interaction appeals to me more than another decorative flourish would. Removing a finished month gives the object a small routine, while keeping the calendar oriented toward what’s coming next.

The clean layout does come with a compromise. This edition has no national public holidays printed, including US holidays. If you’re checking when an office might be closed or planning around a long weekend, you’ll need another reference. I’d miss those markings, even while appreciating the uncluttered presentation. A country-neutral calendar makes sense, but holiday information is genuinely useful.

I haven’t handled a sample, so I can’t judge how securely it stands, how neatly the perforations tear, or how easily the white printing reads under a desk lamp. Those are meaningful questions at this scale. A compact footprint is welcome only if checking the date doesn’t involve pulling the calendar closer every time.

The $20 price makes the decision more about how much you value the object than how urgently you need its function. I like the restraint of the proposition. You get a date reference whose folded construction deserves a closer look, without having to adopt an entirely different planning system. The TriAngular Calendar 2027 can sit beside the laptop and leave the appointments there.

candidates.title: The week in gadgets: the 10 most popular stories
candidates.full_text:
This is the first edition of a weekly chart, and the rule is simple: we don’t pick the ten, you do. Every story below is ranked by its biggest single day in Google Discover this week, pulled from Search Console, and the countdown runs from ten to one.

Saturday rewrote the chart. A classroom robot, two Seikos and a Honda bike took the top off it, and the near-tie that led the early version of this list got pushed down to seventh and eighth.

A note on how the ranking works: a story’s rank is its biggest single day in the feed, not a running total, so a piece that spiked hard on day one can outrank one that simmered all week.

Both kinds are in here. One slot breaks the rule, and it closes the chart at number ten, where the CJRB Spud makes its case with orders instead of clicks.

One entry here didn’t win its slot in the Discover feed: the CJRB Spud .

It won at the checkout. Reah’s October 31 piece on the tiny folder sent readers to Amazon and they kept buying, at a rate no other piece this week came close to matching.

On Friday we rounded up five reasons the Spud keeps selling , built around a 25% price cut that took it to $39.99 from $53.32. We re-checked that price on Amazon this morning and it’s still $39.99, in stock. Small knife, short blade, four-finger grip, and readers keep buying it. That’s a popularity story too, measured in orders instead of clicks.

A compact crossbar-lock folder at $55 on Amazon is the site’s core formula: small knife, real lock, easy price. The price still checks out today, $55 and in stock.

CIVIVI Lil Yonder sat at number one in window after window through Wednesday and Thursday, and on the early version of this chart it stood fourth. Saturday’s surge is the only reason it’s down here.

It also leads our November EDC list , and the feed keeps agreeing with both.

Tuesday’s Dell XPS 13 deal took $200 off and landed at $599.99, and it held the top of the chart for the better part of two days. Deal pieces usually burn fast and die young; this one was still drawing readers days later, because a current XPS at that price needs no sales pitch.

It finished neck and neck with the watch at number seven.

A diver that tracks a second time zone and shrugs off 300 meters of water, the Seiko green-dial Prospex topped the chart in a day and was still in the top five a day later.

It edged out the Dell deal. On Thursday night that fight was for the top of this chart; the weekend’s surge turned it into a fight for seventh, and the watch took this round too.

The Starbucks holiday merch piece ran Friday morning, Bearista cups from $14.95 and the glass cup coming back December 1, and it shot straight to the top of the chart.

It wasn’t a one-day spike either. The piece kept drawing readers straight through Saturday, the kind of legs holiday merch doesn’t usually get in the first week of November.

Saturday’s Benchmade Mini SOCP Folder is a $350 tactical folder built on Greg Thompson’s SOCP design, and it gives you three ways to open the blade: thumb studs, a wave hook and the finger ring. S30V steel, sand G10 scales, swappable ring setups.

Published at midday, it became the strongest knife debut of the week inside its first day.

CIVIVI built its name on folders, and this week it turned to fixed blades: the WoodPal, Thaloryn and Farrow , three drop points with leather sheaths, two of them ground scandi, up for preorder now and shipping November 24.

The WoodPal starts at $74 with a Dutch Bushcraft Knives design credit, the Thaloryn stays under $90 with the thickest stock of the three, and the Farrow runs past $100. The trio posted the biggest knife showing of the week.

Thursday night’s Honda RN0 piece led the early version of this chart. Honda is putting an electric mountain bike in dealerships next to its motorcycles, built with ROTWILD on a carbon monocoque frame with Shimano’s EP810 drive unit, 100 Nm of torque and about 24 kg all in. European motorcycle dealers get it in 2027, test rides and handover included.

It surged about a day after it went live. Two Saturday pieces are the only reason it’s standing at number three.

The Presage Classic Series skips the sunburst finish. The dial is embossed to follow the drape of Tomioka silk, the cloth woven around the Tomioka Silk Mill in Gunma, and it shifts like fabric when the light moves. Three watches run $995 in a new 38mm case, a 2,000-piece limited edition runs $1,150, and the enamel and urushi pair above them runs $1,400 and $1,650.

candidates.title: This Cactus-Inspired Coffee Machine Looks More Like a Sculpture Than a Kitchen Appliance
candidates.full_text:
Most coffee machines are designed to fit in. They sit quietly on kitchen countertops, dressed in familiar shades of black, silver, or white, with little to distinguish one from another. Their purpose is straightforward: make coffee, look reasonably sophisticated, and occupy as little visual attention as possible. But what if a coffee machine had a personality of its own? What if the appliance you reach for every morning could be as expressive as the objects you deliberately choose to decorate your home with? Cacto, a capsule coffee machine, approaches this familiar kitchen essential from an entirely different perspective.

Taking inspiration from the cactus, Cacto brings an unexpected sculptural quality to an appliance that has largely settled into a predictable design language. The cactus is an interesting reference point. It is bold, instantly recognizable, and comfortable standing apart from its surroundings. Its unusual shape gives it character, while its ability to thrive in challenging environments makes it a compelling symbol of independence. These qualities are translated into Cacto’s physical form, creating a coffee machine that feels more like a carefully selected design object than another countertop appliance.

One of the more interesting aspects of Cacto is how its appearance changes depending on where you stand. Its form is designed to offer distinct visual expressions from the front and sides, encouraging people to appreciate the object from multiple perspectives. This consideration makes a difference in how the machine occupies a space. Most kitchen appliances have a clearly defined front, with the remaining surfaces receiving considerably less design attention. Cacto treats the entire object as an opportunity for expression. It is meant to be seen, admired, and kept on display, even when nobody is making coffee.

Behind its unconventional appearance is a philosophy drawn from the idea of the Bourgeois Bohemian, commonly referred to as BoBo. The concept describes individuals who place greater importance on authenticity, independence, and personal experiences than on conventional markers of success. Their choices are guided by what feels meaningful to them, even when those choices challenge popular tastes or expectations. It is a mindset that makes the cactus an especially fitting inspiration. The plant survives through adaptation, maintains its distinctive character, and grows according to the conditions around it without losing its identity.

Cacto uses this connection to explore what individuality might look like in everyday product design. For someone who identifies with the BoBo philosophy, choosing an object for the home is about more than its practical function or perceived status. It is an extension of personal taste. A coffee machine does not necessarily need to disappear into a coordinated kitchen aesthetic to be considered well designed. It can introduce contrast, spark curiosity, and become a small reflection of the person who owns it.

That thinking extends to the experience of making coffee itself. For many people, brewing a cup is one of the first familiar actions of the day, often completed almost automatically while preparing for everything that follows. Cacto invites a slightly different relationship with that routine. Its expressive presence gives the user something to engage with beyond the simple act of preparing a drink. The machine becomes part of a personal ritual, encouraging a moment of attention toward an activity that can otherwise feel entirely ordinary.

There is also something refreshing about the choice to bring such a distinctive personality to a capsule coffee machine. This is an appliance category commonly associated with convenience, efficiency, and compact forms. Cacto retains that familiar product identity while questioning the expectation that convenience should come packaged in a restrained, universally appealing exterior. Its design suggests that even functional objects can accommodate eccentricity and character without needing to justify their presence through additional features.

Cacto’s appeal lies in its willingness to challenge something as familiar as the kitchen coffee machine. It asks why everyday appliances should follow the same visual conventions when the people using them have such different personalities and preferences.
